title: How histories are to be read
source_text: Πρὶν ἀρξώμεθα τῆς ἀπολογίας. λεκτέον ὅτι σχεδὸν πᾶσαν ἱστορίαν, κἂν ἀληθὴς ᾖ, βούλεσθαι κατασκευάζειν ὡς γεγενημένην καὶ καταληπτικὴν ἐμποιῆσαι περὶ αὐτῆς φαντασίαν τῶν σφόδρα ἐστὶ χαλεπωτάτων καὶ (ἐν) ἐνίοις ἀδύνατον. φέρε γάρ τινα λέγειν μὴ γεγονέναι τὸν Ἰλιακὸν πόλεμον μάλιστα διὰ τὸ ἀδύνατον προσπεπλέχθαι λόγον περὶ τοῦ γεγενῆσθαί τινα Ἀχιλλέα θαλασσίας θεᾶς (Θέτιδος) υἱὸν καὶ ἀνθρώπου Πηλέως, ἢ Σαρπηδόνα Διὸς, ἢ Ἀσκάλαφον καὶ Ἰάλμενον Ἄρεος, ἢ Αἰνείαν Ἀφροδίτης· πῶς ἂν κατασκευάσαιμεν τὸ τοιοῦτον, μάλιστα θλιβόμενοι ὑπὸ τοῦ οὐκ οἶδ᾿ ὅπως παρυφανθέντος πλάσματος τῇ κεκρατηκυίᾳ παρὰ πᾶσι δόξῃ περὶ τοῦ ἀληθῶς γεγονέναι τὸν ἐν Ἰλίῳ πόλεμον Ἑλλήνων καὶ Τρώων; φέρε δὲ (καί) τινα ἀπιστεῖν περὶ Οἰδίποδος καὶ Ἰοκάστης καὶ τῶν γεννηθέντων ἀπὸ ἀμφοτέρων Ἐτεοκλέους καὶ Πολυνείκους διὰ τὸ προσπεπλέχθαι τῷ λόγῳ τὴν Σφίγγα μιξοπάρθενόν τινα· πῶς ἂν τὸ τοιοῦτον ἀποδείξαιμεν; οὕτω δὲ καὶ τὰ περὶ τῶν Ἐπιγόνων, κἂν μηδὲν τοιοῦτον ἐπιπεπλεγμένον ᾖ τῷ λόγῳ, ἢ περὶ τῆς Ἡρακλειδῶν καθόδου ἢ περὶ ἄλλων μυρίων. ἀλλ᾿ ὁ εὐγνωμόνως ἐντυγχάνων ταῖς ἱστορίαις καὶ βουλόμενος ἑαυτὸν τηρεῖν καὶ ἐν ἐκείναις ἀνεξαπάτητον κρινεῖ, τίσι μὲν συγκαταθήσεται τίνα δὲ τροπολογήσει, τὸ βούλημα ἐρευνῶν τῶν ἀναπλασαμένων τὰ τοιάδε, καὶ τίσιν ἀπιστήσει ὡς διὰ τὴν πρός τινας χάριν ἀναγεγραμμένοις. καὶ τοῦτο προλαβόντες δι᾿ ὅλην τὴν φερομένην ἐν τοῖς εὐαγγελίοις περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἱστορίαν εἰρήκαμεν, οὐκ ἐπὶ ψιλὴν πίστιν καὶ ἄλογον τοὺς ἐντρεχεστέρους ἐκκαλούμενοι, ἀλλὰ βουλόμενοι παραστῆσαι ὅτι εὐγνωμοσύνης χρεία τοῖς ἐντευξομένοις καὶ πολλῆς ἐξετάσεως καὶ, ἵν᾿ οὕτως ὀνομάσω, εἰσόδου εἰς τὸ βούλημα τῶν γραψάντων, ἵν᾿ εὑρεθῇ, ποίᾳ διανοίᾳ ἕκαστον γέγραπται.
pass_a_gloss: Before we begin the defence (ἀπολογία), it must be said that to wish to establish (κατασκευάζειν) almost every history (ἱστορία), even if it be true, as having happened, and to produce (ἐμποιῆσαι) a cognitive/apprehensive impression (καταληπτικὴν φαντασίαν) about it, is of the very hardest things, and in some impossible. For suppose someone says the Trojan (Ἰλιακόν) war did not happen, especially because of an impossible story (ἀδύνατον λόγον) having been interwoven (προσπεπλέχθαι) about a certain Achilles having been born son of a sea goddess (θαλασσίας θεᾶς) Thetis and a man Peleus, or Sarpedon of Zeus, or Ascalaphus and Ialmenus of Ares, or Aeneas of Aphrodite: how would we establish such a thing, especially being pressed (θλιβόμενοι) by the fiction (πλάσμα) somehow woven in alongside (παρυφανθέντος) the opinion (δόξα) prevailing among all about the Trojan war of Greeks and Trojans having truly happened? And suppose someone disbelieves (ἀπιστεῖν) about Oedipus and Jocasta and those born from both, Eteocles and Polynices, because of the Sphinx, a sort of half-maiden (μιξοπάρθενον), having been interwoven in the story: how would we demonstrate (ἀποδείξαιμεν) such a thing? And so also the things about the Epigoni, even if nothing such is interwoven in the story, or about the return (κάθοδος) of the Heraclidae, or about countless others. But the one who fair-mindedly (εὐγνωμόνως) reads (ἐντυγχάνων) the histories and wishes to keep himself undeceived (ἀνεξαπάτητον) in them too will judge to which he will assent (συγκαταθήσεται), which he will interpret figuratively (τροπολογήσει), searching out the intention (βούλημα) of those who fashioned (ἀναπλασαμένων) such things, and which he will disbelieve as written for favour (χάριν) toward certain people. And anticipating (προλαβόντες) this we have said it on account of the whole history about Jesus carried (φερομένην) in the Gospels, not calling the more skilled (ἐντρεχεστέρους) to bare (ψιλήν) and irrational (ἄλογον) faith (πίστις), but wishing to show that there is need of fair-mindedness (εὐγνωμοσύνη) for those who will read, and of much examination (ἐξέτασις), and, so to name it, of entry (εἴσοδος) into the intention of the writers, so that it may be found with what meaning (διανοίᾳ) each thing has been written.
pass_b_english: Before we begin our defence, it must be said that to try to establish that almost any story, even a true one, actually happened, and to produce a certain and convincing impression about it, is among the very hardest of tasks, and in some cases impossible. Suppose someone says that the Trojan War did not happen, chiefly because an impossible tale has been woven into it, that a certain Achilles was born the son of a sea goddess, Thetis, and of a man, Peleus, or Sarpedon the son of Zeus, or Ascalaphus and Ialmenus the sons of Ares, or Aeneas the son of Aphrodite. How could we establish such a thing, especially when we are hard pressed by the fiction that has somehow been woven into the opinion, held by everyone, that the war at Ilium between the Greeks and the Trojans really happened? Suppose, too, someone disbelieves the story of Oedipus and Jocasta and of Eteocles and Polynices, who were born of them both, because the Sphinx, a kind of half-maiden, has been woven into the tale. How could we prove such a thing? So too with the story of the Epigoni, even though nothing of the kind is woven into it, or with the return of the Heraclidae, or with countless others.

But one who reads histories with fairness, and who wants to keep himself from being deceived even in them, will judge which things he will assent to, which he will take figuratively, searching out the intention of those who invented such things, and which he will disbelieve as written to please certain people. And we have said this in advance with the whole account of Jesus found in the Gospels in view. We are not calling the more intelligent to a bare and unreasoning faith; we want to show that those who are to read them need fairness, much examination, and, if I may call it so, an entering into the intention of the writers, so that it may be found in what sense each thing has been written.

choices.choice: καταληπτικὴ φαντασία is the Stoic technical term for an impression that grasps its object with certainty; rendered 'a certain and convincing impression'. Koetschau's supplements (ἐν) before ἐνίοις, (Θέτιδος) and (καί) are followed. The mythological parentages are Homeric (Achilles, Sarpedon, Aeneas in the Iliad; Ascalaphus and Ialmenus at Iliad 2.512-515), but Origen quotes no line, so no inline classical citation is given. μιξοπάρθενος ('half maiden', i.e. part woman, part beast) is rendered 'a kind of half-maiden' (τινα kept as 'a kind of'). δι᾿ ὅλην ... ἱστορίαν (διά with accusative) is taken as 'with a view to / on account of the whole account of Jesus'. No Scripture is quoted.
'these books' cut to 'them' (τοῖς ἐντευξομένοις has no object)
